newsitem.title: USA: IMF says dangerous to delay EMU.
newsitem.headline: IMF says dangerous to delay EMU.

text.p: Europe is pretty much ready to launch its single currency in 1999 and any delay would be dangerous, an IMF official said on Saturday.

Massimo Russo, special advisor on European monetary union to IMF managing director Michel Camdessus, said delay would create turbulence on financial markets and may lead to the shelving of the project for some time.
"We at the IMF believe a delay ... would lead to substantial dangers," he told a news conference.
Another IMF official also urged European Union leaders to announce early how they plan to fix exchange rates between currencies joining the new euro.
"You can't leave the market without any information whatsoever. Then it would be chaos," Jacques Artus, deputy director of the IMF's European Department, said.

Russo noted that International Monetary Fund forecasts released on Wednesday showed all EU countries except Greece were near to fulfilling Maastricht treaty criteria for entry to Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) at its launch.
"The conditions for a successful start of EMU are largely in place," he said.

The forecasts, contained in the IMF's latest World Economic Outlook, showed Germany, France and Italy all showing a public deficit equivalent to 3.3 percent of gross domestic product in 1997 in the absence of new measures.
He also said it did not matter whether countries cut their public deficits precisely to three percent of GDP, provided they came near.
"I don't believe 3.1 percent makes the euro weak and 2.9 percent makes the euro strong," he said.

What also mattered, he said, was that countries should show their deficit reductions were sustainable. This is a key worry about Italy which has imposed a one-off euro tax to meet the deficit criteria this year.

EU leaders will decide in late April/early May 1998 which countries qualify for monetary union, based on actual economic and fiscal performances in 1997, and on an assessment of the sustainability of their policies in the years to come.
Russo said Italy still had time to ensure its deficit did not rise again in 1998 and urged it to take action on pension reform and cut spending on welfare and public sector workers.
"There is time to adopt the measures that would bring the deficit in 1998 below three percent," he said.

Both Russo and Artus warned of the need to act to head of financial market turbulence in the period between the decision on which countries qualify to join and the irrevocable locking of exchange rates when the euro is launched in 1999.
"My understanding is that something will be done to address this issue," Russo said.
EU officials have said that though technically exchange rates cannot be fixed until the end of 1998, governments could announce early the method for fixing rates.
This would have the effect of a self-fulfilling phrophecy whereby markets pushed currencies to the rates implied by the chosen method when the euro is launched.
Officials have suggested either using central rates in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) or an average of market rates over a period of time.
"There are various alternatives which are being considered right now. It would be useful to announce ahead of time how it will be done," Artus said.
"It is likely that at the time you take the decision on (EMU) membership that you announce the methodology," he said.
And before the decision is made on which countries can join, the best way of heading off currency turbulence was to continue efforts to bring Europe's economies into line.

"If policies and fundamentals do not indicate the countries converging, I don't see what can be done. The best assurance against market speculation is not to give any reason for an attack to start," Russo said.
